'''Awaga Daimyōjin Mototsufumi''' (粟鹿大明神元記) is an {{ill|komonjo|ja|古文書|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/ancient document|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q89298567}} passed down by the shrine families of {{ill|Awaga Shrine|ja|粟鹿神社|zh|粟鹿神社|qid=Q11604651|lt=Awaga Shrine}} in {{ill|Tajima Province|en|Tajima Province|qid=Q1053727|lt=Tajima Province}}, {{ill|Asago District, Hyōgo|ceb|Asako-gun|fa|شهرستان آساگو، هیوگو|ja|朝来郡|zh|朝來郡|qid=Q4803324|lt=Asago District, Tajima}} (present-day {{ill|Hyōgo Prefecture|en|Hyōgo Prefecture|qid=Q130290|lt=Hyōgo Prefecture}}).
== Overview ==
Compiled in the first year of {{ill|Wadō (era)|en|Wadō (era)|qid=Q1373026|lt=Wadō}} ({{ill|708|en|708|qid=Q23511|lt=708}}), the text was authored by {{ill|Jinbu no Sukune Nemaro|ja|神部直根麻呂}}, also known as the {{ill|Shinra General|ja|新羅将軍}} and holder of the court Rank of Junior Sixth Rank, Upper Grade. The document details the enshrined deity {{ill|Ame-no-Misari-no-Mikoto|ja|天美佐利命}} and the origins of Awaga Shrine. It also contains a vertical lineage chart tracing the genealogy of the {{ill|Jinbu clan|ja|神部氏}}, descendants of {{ill|Izanagi|en|Izanagi|qid=Q813858|lt=Izanagi}} and {{ill|Izanami|en|Izanami|qid=Q682306|lt=Izanami}}. If the date of origin is accurate, it would predate the compilation of the {{ill|Kojiki|en|Kojiki|qid=Q813031|lt=Kojiki}} and {{ill|Nihon Shoki|en|Nihon Shoki|qid=Q813935|lt=Nihon Shoki}}, although there are dissenting opinions regarding its authenticity.{{Sfn|Maenosono|1977|pp=115–147}}{{Sfn|Sema|1989|pp=1–34}}
The document was originally stored in the archives of the {{ill|Kujō family|en|Kujō family|qid=Q1791350|lt=Kujō family}}. It was rediscovered in {{ill|1955|en|1955|qid=Q18577|lt=Showa 30}} by Kōzō Korezawa and is now housed in the {{ill|Archives and Mausolea Department|en|Archives and Mausolea Department|qid=Q4346533|lt=Archives and Mausolea Department}} of the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|en|Imperial Household Agency|qid=Q1143602|lt=Imperial Household Agency}}.{{Sfn|Maenosono|1977|pp=115–147}}
== Research ==
Kōzō Korezawa discovered the Kujō Family’s ''Mototsufumi'' and noted that a different version, the Tanimori manuscript, was also cataloged in the Shoryōbu archives. Between 1955 and 1958, he published three key papers: ''The 11ly Discovered Deity of Awaga Shrine,'' ''Research on the Awaga Daimyōjin Mototsufumi'' (Parts I and II), and ''On the Awaga Daimyōjin Mototsufumi of Tajima Province, Asago District.'' His studies emphasized the following:
* The Kujō manuscript is a copy made during the {{ill|Kamakura period|en|Kamakura period|qid=Q236205|lt=Kamakura period}} or early {{ill|Muromachi period|en|Muromachi period|qid=Q334845|lt=Muromachi period}}.
* The deity enshrined at Awaga Shrine was originally {{ill|Ame-no-Misari-no-Mikoto|ja|天美佐利命}}, contrary to confusion in the medieval period.
* The date of the document’s compilation, Wadō 1 (708), aligns with the {{ill|Jitō era}} edict for clans such as the {{ill|Miwa clan|ja|大三輪氏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōmiwa clan|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大神氏|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大神氏|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11438330}} to present their genealogies. The ''Mototsufumi'' is closely connected to these records.
* The compiler, Jinbu no Sukune Nemaro, is likely identical to the ''Miwa no Kimi Nemaro'' mentioned in the ''Nihon Shoki'' entry for {{ill|Tenji 2|ja|天智2年}}.
* Its vertical lineage chart predates comparable genealogical records such as those in the {{ill|Waki clan genealogy|ja|和気氏系図}} and the {{ill|Ama-no-Miwa genealogy|ja|天野系図}}, making it a valuable source.
* While there are inconsistencies, such as the presence of {{ill|Posthumous name|en|Posthumous name|qid=Q696100|lt=Chinese-style posthumous titles}} and place names incompatible with its purported date, the original manuscript remains a vital historical and linguistic artifact.{{Sfn|Korezawa|1955|pp=133–196}}{{Sfn|Korezawa|1956|pp=31–73}}{{Sfn|Korezawa|1957|pp=1–17}}{{Sfn|Korezawa|1958|pp=40–64}}
Several scholars, including {{ill|Takashi Tanaka|ja|田中卓|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Takashi Tanaka|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11575370}}, recognized its significance in tracing the genealogy of ancient clans and its connections to the ''{{ill|Nihon Shoki}}'' and ''{{ill|Kujiki|en|Kujiki|qid=Q2716751|lt=Sendai Kuji Hongi}}''.{{Sfn|Tanaka|1956|pp=91–113}}
